blocks.text: In the pudendal nerve block, the nerve is infiltrated with a local anaesthetic at the point where it crosses the ischial spine using a needle inserted through the vaginal wall, directed by a finger. It aids in achieving almost painless vaginal or forceps deliveries and is also helpful for minor surgeries involving the vagina and perineum.

When a bilateral pudendal block is administered, it results in a loss of the anal reflex (saddle anaesthesia), relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles, and diminished sensation in the vulva and lower third of the vagina.

items.text: **Lesser sciatic notch (Option A)** is the area where the pudendal nerve exits the gluteal region and enters the pudendal canal. It's not easily accessible for the nerve block.
**Pubic symphysis (Option B):** Administering the block here would not accurately target the pudendal nerve and is unlikely to deliver the intended analgesic effect for perineal pain.
**Greater sciatic notch (Option C):** is the point from which the pudendal nerve enters the gluteal region; it is not the preferred site for nerve block.

blocks.text: Pudendal nerve originates in the pelvis from the anterior rami of the S2, S3 and S4 nerves of the sacral plexus. It enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic notch, curves behind the ischial spine for a brief distance, and exits the gluteal area by passing into the lesser sciatic foramen.

items.text: **Greater sciatic foramen → Obturator foramen (Option A):** Obturator foramen is related to the obturator nerve, not the pudendal nerve.

**Lesser sciatic foramen → Greater sciatic foramen (Option B):** This reverses the actual order. The nerve first exits via the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters through the lesser, not the other way around.
**Obturator foramen → Lesser sciatic foramen (Option C):** The pudendal nerve doesn't use the obturator foramen. The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh, not the perineum.

blocks.text: Ischiorectal Fossa/Ischioanal Fossa: Is a space filled with fat lateral to the anal canal and just below the pelvic diaphragm. Has a shape of a triangular pyramid, with the apex at the boundary of the anal canal and the obturator fascia and the base directed towards the perineal surface. Divided into the perianal space and the ischiorectal space by the perineal fascia.
Anatomy and Boundaries
**Location:** Situated on either side of the anal canal and extends from the skin of the perineum to the pelvic diaphragm.
Boundaries

items.text: **Medially**
External anal sphincter
Levator ani (muscles of the pelvic floor)
**Laterally**
Obturator internus muscle
Ischial tuberosity
**Anteriorly**
Pubic symphysis and puborectalis muscle.
**Posteriorly**
Sacrotuberous ligament and gluteus maximus muscle.

blocks.text: Subcutaneous fat is abundant on both sides of the anal canal, which permits distension of the anal canal during defecation.
Clinical Significance

items.text: **Abscess Formation:** Ischioanal abscesses can occur due to infection, leading to significant pain and swelling in the perineal area.
**Surgical Access:** Knowledge of the ischiorectal fossa is important for surgical procedures in the anal region, such as drainage of abscesses or repair of fistulas.
**Fecal Incontinence:** Injury to the neurovascular structures in this area can lead to issues with anal control.

blocks.text: The most common site of urethral rupture is at the bulb of the penis, typically caused by trauma such as a fall onto a sharp object. In this case, the urethra is crushed against the pubic bones. Urine then leaks into the superficial perineal pouch and spreads over the scrotum, penis, and anterior abdominal wall beneath the membranous layer of the superficial fascia (superficial extravasation).

items.text: **Membranous urethra (Option A):** Located above the urogenital diaphragm, an injury here would cause urine to leak into the deep perineal pouch, not into the superficial perineal structures.
**Prostatic urethra (Option B):** An injury to the prostatic urethra would involve the deep perineal structures and extraperitoneal space, not the scrotum or anterior abdominal wall.

blocks.text: External urethral sphincter is located in the deep perineal pouch and plays a critical role in controlling urinary continence. Deep perineal pouch is in the urogenital triangle of the perineum below the pelvic diaphragm. It presents as a triangular, trilaminar space with sphincter urethrae [external urethral sphincter], deep transverse perineal, and compressor urethrae [in females].
**Boundaries of the Deep Perineal Pouch:**

items.text: **Superior boundary (roof):** Pelvic diaphragm (levator ani).
**Inferior boundary (floor):** Perineal membrane (inferior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm).
**Lateral boundary:** Inferior portions of the obturator internus muscle and the ischiopubic rami.

blocks.text: **Contents of the Deep Perineal Pouch:**

rows: Muscles and Glands

External urethral sphincter: Surrounds the membranous part of the urethra and controls the voluntary release of urine.
Deep transverse perineal muscle: Provides structural support to the perineum.
Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands: Small glands that secrete pre-ejaculate fluid into the urethra.

Membranous urethra: Part of the urethra that passes through the deep perineal pouch.
External urethral sphincter: Surrounds the urethra and controls voluntary urination.
Deep transverse perineal muscle: Provides support to the perineum and helps maintain the integrity of the pelvic floor.
Compressor urethrae muscle: Aids in urinary continence by compressing the urethra.
Urethrovaginal sphincter: Wraps around the urethra and vagina, assisting in control over the urethra.
Nerves and Vessels
Branches of the dorsal nerve and artery of the penis, along with the pudendal nerve branches.
Branches of the internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve supplying the clitoris and surrounding regions.

blocks.text: **Functions:**

items.text: **Urinary continence:** The external urethral sphincter plays a key role in controlling urination, helping to retain urine voluntarily.
**Support of pelvic structures:** The muscles of the deep perineal pouch help support the perineum and pelvic organs.
**Sexual function:** In males, the bulbourethral glands secrete fluid that lubricates the urethra during sexual arousal.

blocks.text: Pubic symphysis is located at the anterior aspect of the perineum and is easily palpated when the patient is in the lithotomy position.
**View from Lithotomy Position:**
Bones and Anatomical Landmarks

items.text: **Pubic Symphysis:** Located at the anterior aspect of the pelvis and acts as the anterior boundary of the perineum.

**Ischiopubic Rami:** They form the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle and are important as attachment points for muscles like the ischiocavernosus and the deep and superficial perineal muscles.
**Ischial Tuberosities:** They serve as the lateral borders of the anal triangle.

blocks.text: In the lithotomy position, the ischial tuberosities can be palpated as they provide attachment points for the superficial transverse perineal muscles and are important in identifying the perineal body.

items.text: **Coccyx:** The small, triangular bone at the base of the spine, forming the posterior border of the pelvic outlet and provides an attachment point for the coccygeus muscle.
**Sacrum:** Lies posteriorly and superiorly, forming the posterior wall of the pelvic cavity.
**Obturator Foramen:** A large opening formed by the pubis and ischium which allows the passage of the obturator nerve and vessels.

blocks.text: **Perineal Regions Related to Bones:** From the lithotomy position, the perineal area can be divided into the urogenital triangle and the anal triangle.
**Muscles Attached to Bony Landmarks (Visible from Lithotomy Position):**

items.text: **Levator Ani (Pubococcygeus, Iliococcygeus):** Support the pelvic organs and form part of the pelvic diaphragm.
**Ischiocavernosus and Bulbospongiosus:** Attach to the ischiopubic rami and help in erection (males) and clitoral function (females).
**Superficial and Deep Transverse Perineal Muscles:** Attach to the ischial tuberosities and the perineal body, providing support to the pelvic floor.

blocks.text: If the rupture occurs above the urogenital diaphragm, urine escapes into the deep perineal pouch and may spread upward around the prostate and bladder into the extraperitoneal space (deep extravasation). Here, the membranous urethra is located above the urogenital diaphragm. A high-riding prostate could be further suggestive of posterior urethral injury, though not a reliable indicator.

Patient’s symptoms of increased urinary frequency, nocturia, and difficulty initiating urination, along with the finding of an enlarged prostate, are classic signs of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
**Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH):** Non-malignant enlargement or hyperplasia of the prostate tissue. Common in older men, particularly those over 50 and prevalence increases with age.
Hyperplasia results from impaired cell death, resulting in the accumulation of senescent cells in the prostate.
Pathophysiology

items.text: Hormonal changes (increased dihydrotestosterone, DHT) contribute to prostate growth.
Proliferation of stromal and epithelial cells, and delayed epithelial cell death in the transitional zone.

blocks.text: Diagnosis

items.text: Digital rectal exam (DRE) reveals enlarged prostate.
Urinalysis to rule out infection.
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test to assess for prostate cancer.
Urinary flow rate tests can evaluate the severity of obstruction.
24 hour voiding diary
Urodynamics

items.text: Acute urinary retention
Urinary tract infections
Bladder stones
Kidney damage (if untreated)

blocks.text: Treatment

items.text: Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride).
Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
Transurethral incision of the prostate
Transurethral electrovaporization
Holmium and Thulium laser enucleation of the prostate
**Prostate cancer (Option A)** presents similarly but would typically require further evaluation and would more likely present with nodularity or firmness rather than a smooth enlarged prostate.
**Prostatitis (Option B):** causes urinary symptoms but usually associated with pain, fever or dysuria.
**Urinary tract infection (Option D):** causes urinary frequency and urgency but would usually be associated with other symptoms like dysuria or fever.

blocks.text: Prostatic Urethra
Segment of the male urethra that passes through the prostate gland.
Location

items.text: Widest part of male urethra. (Option B)
Contains urethral crest, seminal colliculus, prostatic utricle and orifices of prostatic duct.
Extends from the bladder neck to the beginning of the membranous urethra which is approximately 3-4 cm in length. (Option C)

blocks.text: Histology
Urothelium immediately surrounded by glandular and strong tissue of the periurethral zone of the prostate. (Option A)
Functions
Conducts urine from the bladder to the external urethral orifice and serves as a passage for semen during ejaculation. (Option D)
Associated Structures
Receives the ejaculatory ducts, which deliver semen from the seminal vesicles and the vas deferens and contains the prostatic urethral orifices, which allow for the secretion of prostatic fluid.
Clinical Significance

Can be affected by conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostate cancer, leading to urinary obstruction. Digital rectal examination (DRE) can assess the prostate’s condition via the prostatic urethra.

While performing uterine artery ligation, ‘ water under bridge ’ can occur due to injury to Ureter. ‘Water’ refers to urine, due to leak from the ureter and ‘bridge’ is formed by the uterine artery. Ureter lies posteroinferior to the uterine artery.
Relations of Arteries with Ureter
Uterine artery is a branch of anterior division of internal iliac artery and ovarian artery is a branch of abdominal aorta, both of which anastomose.

Uterine artery is anterosuperior to the ureter by 2.5 cm and then crosses the ureter to ascend along the lateral side of the uterus. Ureter passes forward, just above the lateral fornix of the vagina, and lies about 2 cm to the side of the supravaginal portion of the cervix. It then curves inward toward the urinary bladder, coming into close contact with the vagina.

While performing hysterectomy, careful ligation of the uterine artery should be done to prevent this. Presence of peristaltic movements and the pale glistening appearance with firm cord feel on palpation will help in identifying the ureter.
Mesenteries Supporting Female Reproductive System

items.text: **Broad ligament**
Fold of peritoneum attaching uterus to the lateral pelvic wall
**Mesovarium**
Attaches ovary to the posterior layer of broad ligament
**Mesometrium**
Part of broad ligament lying between uterine tube and ovarian ligament (Ovarian ligament: passes from lower pole of ovary to lateral angle of uterus)
**Suspensory Ligament of the Ovary**
Part of the broad ligament that stretches from the upper pole of the ovary and the infundibulum of the uterine tube to the lateral pelvic wall
Also known as infundibulopelvic ligament

blocks.text: Angle shown in the image between the cervix and vagina is known as the Angle of Anteversion. Angle between the uterus and cervix is known as the Angle of Anteflexion.
Uterus is maintained in an anteverted state mainly by Round ligament with minor contribution from uterosacral ligament in non-pregnant female. (Hence, Option C would be most appropriate)
Angle of Anteversion & Anteflexion

items.text: **Angle of Anteversion**
Description: Angle between long axis of cervix and long axis of vagina
Angle Normal: 90°
Maintained by Non-pregnant female: Round ligament (main) + uterosacral ligament (Option C)
Pregnant female: Round ligament only
**Angle of Anteflexion**
Description: Angle between long axis of uterus and long axis of cervix
Angle Normal: 120°-170°
Maintained by Uterosacral ligament

blocks.text: Pelvic Fascia
The pelvic fascia is categorized into sections covering the pelvic wall, floor, and viscera.

items.text: **Fascia of the Pelvic Wall:** Tough and membranous, covering the obturator internus and piriformis muscles and attaching to the bone margins.
**Fascia of the Pelvic Floor:** Looser and less dense, covered by the parietal layer of pelvic fascia.
**Fascia Surrounding the Pelvic Viscera:** Loosely structured, often containing areolar tissue, allowing for the distension of pelvic organs.

blocks.text: **Deep Endopelvic Connective Tissue Condenses to Form the Following Ligaments:**

items.text: **Mackenrodt’s Ligaments**
Formed by condensation of parietal fascia covering the obturator internus.
Distal part of the ureter passes under the uterine artery within the upper part of the cardinal ligament.
Function: Lateral stabilization to the cervix at the level of ischial spine.
**Uterosacral Ligaments**
Formed by condensation of peritoneum.
They hold the cervix posteriorly at the level of the ischial spines and the uterus in Anteflexed state.
**Pubocervical Fascia (Bladder Pillar)**
Serve mainly as vascular conduit.
Extensions:
Rectovaginal septum: known as Fascia of Denonvilliers’
Pubocervical ring: encircles supravaginal part of cervix
Vesicovaginal septum: supports bladder and anterior vaginal wall
**Round Ligament**
Runs anterior to obturator artery and lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
Main ligament responsible for maintaining the uterus in Anteverted state.
Embryologically, it corresponds with the gubernaculum of testis.
In the fetus, the peritoneum continuing with the round ligament in the inguinal region is known as Canal of Nuck.
**Ovarian Ligament**
Morphologically continuous with the round ligament and is homologous to the gubernaculum of testis.

blocks.text: The marked structures in the histological image are cilia. Cilia are slender, hair-like structures found on the surface of many epithelial cells. They play a vital role in the movement of fluids and particles along various passageways in the body. While the epithelial lining of the epididymis does have stereocilia (long microvilli), it does not typically have cilia.
Surface Projections

items.text: **Microvilli:** Small finger-like projections (~1 micrometer) that increase surface area, found in the brush border of the kidney, gall bladder, and intestinal cells.
**Stereocilia:** Long microvilli (15-20 micrometers) located in the hair cells of the inner ear and the epididymis in the male reproductive tract.
**Cilia:** Motile cilia (7-10 micrometers) propel substances along the surface of certain epithelia.

blocks.text: Non-motile cilia, present on nearly every cell in the G0 stage, were once considered nonfunctional but are now known to play a role in signaling pathways during both development and adulthood.
**Oviduct, Bronchi, Ependyma (Options A, C, and D):** have cilia in their epithelial lining.

The A point marked on the image of the femur is the lesser trochanter of the femur. The Iliopsoas muscle arises from the Iliac fossa and lumbar spine and attaches to the lesser trochanter of the femur. Iliopsoas is a large compound muscle of the inner hip composed of the iliacus and psoas major muscles. It is situated on the posterior abdominal wall. The iliopsoas muscle is the primary flexor of the hip joint.
It is also responsible for external hip rotation at the hip joint. It causes flexion of the trunk at the hip, lateral flexion of the trunk (psoas major only)
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Gluteus maximus (Option A):** is the largest and heaviest muscle in the body. It takes its origin from the dorsum of the hip bone as well as from the dorsum of the sacrum and also has ligaments. Insertion is on the gluteal tuberosity on the posterior aspect of the upper femur bone.

**Quadriceps femoris (Option C):** are the group of muscles in front of the thigh. Quadriceps perform a variety of movements, including running, jumping, kicking, and walking. There are 4 Quadriceps: Rectus femoris. Vastus lateralis Vastus medialis Vastus intermedius. When Quadriceps muscles contract, they extend the knee joint, straightening the leg. The quadriceps femoris attaches to the patella via the quadriceps tendon and does not attach to the lesser trochanter, so this is incorrect.

**Adductor Magnus (Option D):** is a prime mover of the femur into adduction. One portion of the adductor muscle flexes the thigh and works as a medial rotator; the other extends the thigh and is a lateral rotator. The adductor magnus attaches to the adductor tubercle on the femur, not the lesser trochanter, so this is also incorrect.
